hints: Think about what charge an amino acid has when its $\text{-COO}^{-}$ and $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ groups exactly balance each other.
walkthrough:
Picture the zwitterion balance**
Think of an amino acid as able to gain or lose $\text{H}^{+}$. At low pH it is cationic, at high pH it is anionic. In the middle there is one special pH where the positive and negative charges cancel to give no net charge. That neutral dipolar ion is the zwitterion, for example $\text{H}_{3}\text{N}^{+}\text{CH(R)COO}^{-}$.
Final answer: The pH at which the amino acid exists as a zwitterion with zero overall charge.

hints: Compare pH 2 with the isoelectric points 5.41 and 2.77 to decide whether each amino acid will be protonated to a cation or deprotonated to an anion.

Recall which groups accept $\text{H}^{+}$ at low pH, the $\text{-COO}^{-}$ to $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ to $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$, and check whether the side chain $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ is basic.
walkthrough:
Decide cation or anion**
You are at pH 2, which is well below 5.41 for asparagine and below 2.77 for aspartic acid. Low pH means excess $\text{H}^{+}$, so both molecules pick up protons to become overall positive cations.

Protonate the backbone**
Start from the neutral forms given. The $\text{-NH}_{2}$ group becomes $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and any $\text{-COO}^{-}$ present in a zwitterion becomes $\text{-COOH}$. So the alpha part becomes $\text{HOOCCH(NH}_{3}^{+}\text{)}$ in both cases.

Leave the neutral side chains as they are**
The asparagine side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ is an amide, not basic enough to protonate at pH 2, so it stays unchanged. The aspartic acid side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ is already fully protonated as $\text{-COOH}$ at this low pH. Add the overall $+$ charge outside the brackets.

Final answer: asparagine at pH 2: $[\text{HOOCCH(NH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}]^{+}$
aspartic acid at pH 2: $[\text{HOOCCH(NH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{COOH}]^{+}$

hints: Recall the two separate reducing actions of excess $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$: $\text{-COOH}$ gives $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ gives $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$.
Apply those changes to each functional group in asparagine and aspartic acid while leaving the alpha $\text{-NH}_{2}$ group unchanged.
walkthrough:
Sort the reducible groups**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is a powerful reducing agent. It converts a carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ right down to a primary alcohol $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, and it converts an amide $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ right down to an amine $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. The simple amine $\text{-NH}_{2}$ on the alpha carbon is not reduced.

Reduce asparagine**
Asparagine $\text{HOOCCH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ has one acid and one amide. The acid end becomes $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)-}$ and the side chain amide becomes $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Join them to give $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, a diamino alcohol.

Reduce aspartic acid**
Aspartic acid $\text{HOOCCH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ has two acids. Both become $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ groups, giving $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, an amino diol.

Final answer: product from asparagine: $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$
product from aspartic acid: $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$

hints: Remember that each $\text{-COOH}$ needs one $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ to become $\text{-COCl}$, releasing $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$.
walkthrough:
Balance the double conversion**
Propanedioic acid has two $\text{-COOH}$ groups, so you need two molecules of $\text{SOCl}_{2}$. Each $\text{-OH}$ is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ to give $\text{ClOCCH}_{2}\text{COCl}$, and the byproducts are $2\text{SO}_{2} + 2\text{HCl}$. Check atoms balance on both sides.
Final answer: $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{COOH} + 2\text{SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{ClOCCH}_{2}\text{COCl} + 2\text{SO}_{2} + 2\text{HCl}$

hints: Identify which group on asparagine attacks the $\text{-COCl}$ groups, the nucleophilic alpha $\text{-NH}_{2}$ to form a new $\text{-NHCO-}$ amide link.

Use the formula $\text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{16}\text{N}_{4}\text{O}_{8}$ and the clue of four amide groups to see that one central $\text{-COCH}_{2}\text{CO-}$ unit must join two whole asparagine molecules.
walkthrough:
Spot the nucleophile**
With excess asparagine, the alpha $\text{-NH}_{2}$ acts as the nucleophile toward the highly electrophilic $\text{-COCl}$ carbon. Each $\text{-COCl}$ loses $\text{Cl}$ as $\text{HCl}$ and forms $\text{-CONH-}$. The $\text{-COOH}$ and side chain $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ of asparagine do not react under these conditions.

Build the bridged molecule**
One $\text{ClOCCH}_{2}\text{COCl}$ has two ends, so it reacts with two asparagine molecules. Put $\text{-COCH}_{2}\text{CO-}$ in the centre, then attach $\text{-NHCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$ on each side. That gives $\text{HOOCCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NHCOCH}_{2}\text{CONHCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$.

Check the amide count**
Count amides: two new central $\text{-NHCO-}$ links plus two untouched side chain $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ groups equals four amide groups, matching the description and the molecular formula $\text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{16}\text{N}_{4}\text{O}_{8}$.

Final answer: $\text{HOOCCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NHCOCH}_{2}\text{CONHCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)COOH}$, with two new amide links plus the two original side chain amides, total four amides.

hints: Recall that hot excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ hydrolyses an amide $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ to a carboxylate $\text{-COO}^{-}$ plus $\text{NH}_{3}$.
Remember that any $\text{-COOH}$ group is also deprotonated to $\text{-COO}^{-}$ in excess alkali, while $\text{-NH}_{2}$ remains as $\text{-NH}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the side chain amide**
Think of the side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ breaking at the $\text{C-N}$ bond by addition of $\text{OH}^{-}$. It becomes $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{COO}^{-}$ and releases $\text{NH}_{3}$.

Deprotonate the acid**
In excess hot $\text{NaOH}$, the alpha $\text{-COOH}$ cannot survive as an acid. It is neutralised to $\text{-COO}^{-}$. The alpha $\text{-NH}_{2}$ stays as $\text{-NH}_{2}$ in strong base, it is not protonated. The full organic anion is therefore $\text{}^{-}\text{OOCCH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{COO}^{-}$.
Final answer: $\text{}^{-}\text{OOCCH(NH}_{2}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{COO}^{-}$ (with $2\text{Na}^{+}$ as counter ions, $\text{NH}_{3}$ also formed)

hints: Identify the two groups in asparagine that can condense, the alpha $\text{-COOH}$ of one monomer and the alpha $\text{-NH}_{2}$ of the next, with loss of water.
Keep the side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ unchanged on every residue when drawing the backbone $\text{-CO-CH-NH-}$ sequence.
Remember to extend the chain with trailing bonds at each end and to bracket one full $\text{-CO-CH-NH-}$ unit as the repeat unit.
walkthrough:
Choose the polymerising groups**
Only the backbone $\text{-COOH}$ and alpha $\text{-NH}_{2}$ form the polymer links. The side chain $\text{-CONH}_{2}$ is an amide already and does not condense further. Each condensation loses $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to give a new peptide style $\text{-CONH-}$ link.

Draw three residues in a row**
Line up three monomers head to tail: $\text{-CO-CH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)-NH-CO-CH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)-NH-CO-CH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)-NH-}$. Show every $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ side chain explicitly. Put free trailing bonds at the left $\text{-CO-}$ end and the right $\text{-NH-}$ end to show continuation.

Mark the repeat unit**
Bracket one repeating block containing one $\text{CO}$, one $\text{CH}$ with its side chain, and one $\text{NH}$, that is $\text{-COCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NH-}$. Label it repeat unit. This shows how the long chain is built from identical asparagine residues.

Final answer: Polyamide: $\text{-COCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NH-COCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NH-COCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NH-}$ with trailing bonds; repeat unit $\text{-COCH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)NH-}$ clearly labelled.

hints: Recall that the two optically active forms are non-superimposable mirror images with identical physical properties except for interaction with polarised light.
Think about what is the same (rotation occurs, magnitude equal) and what is opposite (clockwise vs anticlockwise) when pure enantiomers of equal concentration are compared.
walkthrough:
Link optical activity to enantiomers**
Aspartic acid has a chiral centre at the alpha carbon, so it exists as a pair of enantiomers. Both enantiomers are optically active, meaning each will rotate the plane of plane polarised light.

Separate same from opposite**
Because they are mirror images measured at the same concentration, the size of the rotation is identical, that is the two similarities. The only difference is the sense of rotation: if one rotates light to the right, the other rotates it to the left by exactly the same number of degrees.

Final answer: Similarities: both rotate the plane of plane polarised light; by the same angle (for same concentration and path length).
Difference: in opposite directions (one clockwise, one anticlockwise).

hints: Recall the special name for a 50:50 mixture of enantiomers that is optically inactive overall.
walkthrough:
Name the equal mixture**
When you mix exactly equal amounts of the two enantiomers, their equal and opposite rotations cancel out. This optically inactive 50:50 mixture is called a racemic mixture.
Final answer: racemic mixture (racemate)
